definition: In philosophy and artificial intelligence (especially, knowledge based systems), the ramification problem is concerned with the indirect consequences of an action.
details: It might also be posed as how to represent what happens implicitly due to an action or how to control the secondary and tertiary effects of an action. It is strongly connected to, and is opposite the qualification side of, the frame problem. Limit theory helps in operational usage. For instance, in KBE derivation of a populated design (geometrical objects, etc., similar concerns apply in shape theory), equivalence assumptions allow convergence where potentially large, and perhaps even computationally indeterminate, solution sets are handled deftly. Yet, in a chain of computation, downstream events may very well find some types of results from earlier resolutions of ramification as problematic for their own algorithms.

explainer.lead: The ramification problem is how to capture the indirect consequences of an action in a knowledge-based representation. It matters because ignoring secondary and tertiary effects leaves a model of a dynamic world wrong after every action.

tiers.eli5: If you unplug a lamp, the light goes out — but also the room gets dark and you might trip. The ramification problem is about teaching a computer to notice all those knock-on effects, not just the first one.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers building action models must decide which indirect effects to represent explicitly and which to leave implicit; neglecting them produces inconsistent states after actions. A common pitfall is losing control of secondary and tertiary effects, causing the model to explode.
tiers.paperLevel: Concerned with the indirect consequences of an action and how to represent what happens implicitly or control its secondary and tertiary effects. It is strongly connected to, and opposite the qualification side of, the frame problem; limit theory helps in operational usage.

explainer.example: In knowledge-based engineering derivation of a populated design, equivalence assumptions allow convergence where the space of effects is potentially large, even computationally intractable; similar concerns apply in shape theory.
